query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A minor micro‐alloying addition of boron (≈1–2 at.%) into phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy or compositionally complex alloys will improve glass‐forming ability and enhance the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
generation.material_initial_state: A phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy (or compositionally complex) alloy produced via rapid solidification that shows marginal amorphous phase formation and limited thermal stability of the amorphous state.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled boron addition (~1–2 atomic percent) into the alloy's composition prior to processing.
generation.conditions: Under rapid solidification conditions that ensure homogeneous distribution of boron, the intervention is anticipated to improve glass formation; however, if cooling rates are too low or boron is added in excess, the effect may not manifest.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced local atomic packing and short-range chemical order mediated by boron interacting with phosphorus and the other principal elements, leading to increased atomic size mismatch.
generation.mechanism: The boron addition is expected to frustrate crystallization kinetics by increasing atomic size disparity and chemical bonding complexity, thereby raising the energy barrier for nucleation and growth of crystalline phases during cooling and subsequent thermal exposure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline, the boron‐modified alloy should display a lower critical cooling rate for glass formation and a higher crystallization onset temperature (Tx) in DSC measurements, indicating improved thermal stability of the amorphous state.
generation.baseline: The phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloy processed without any boron addition.
generation.boundary: This improvement is anticipated only within a narrow boron concentration window (≈1–2 at.%); outside this range or in alloys lacking sufficient atomic size mismatch, the intervention may not have a discernible effect.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the improvement in glass-forming ability and thermal stability, as well as the interplay with other alloying elements, remains to be empirically determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two alloy sets: one set of phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloys with a 1–2 at.% boron addition and a control set without boron. Both sets should be processed under identical rapid solidification conditions to produce as‐quenched samples. Characterize the samples using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to assess glass transition and crystallization onset temperatures and X‐ray diffraction (XRD) to determine the presence of amorphous versus crystalline phases.
measurements: DSC to record the glass transition temperature, crystallization onset temperature (Tx), and quantify the exothermic crystallization heat flow
Critical cooling rate assessments to determine the minimum rate required for amorphization
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-containing alloys do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in the critical cooling rate for glass formation and/or do not show an increased crystallization onset temperature (Tx) relative to the control, then the hypothesis will be falsified.
